summary.text: Taking \(n=7\), the conditions \(x\le y\le z\) and \(x+y+z=7\) imply \(3x\le7\), hence \(x\le2\). This contradicts \(x\in\{3,4,6,10,15\}\), so the strengthened representation claim already fails at \(7\).

full_proof.text:
Let the claimed statement be the conjunction, for every natural number \(n\), of the following two assertions:

1. if \(n>5\), then \(a(n)>0\), where \(a(n)\) counts positive ordered triples \(x\le y\le z\) with \(x+y+z=n\) for which
\[
2x-1,\quad 2y-1,\quad 2z-1,\quad 2xy-1,\quad 2xz-1,\quad 2yz-1
\]
are all prime;

2. if \(n>6\), then there is such a triple for which, in addition,
\[
x\in\{3,4,6,10,15\}.
\]

We disprove the universal statement by taking \(n=7\). Certainly \(7>6\), so the second assertion would require natural numbers \(x,y,z\) satisfying all of the following:
\[
x>0,\qquad y>0,\qquad z>0,
\]
\[
x+y+z=7,
\]
\[
x\le y\le z,
\]
and
\[
x\in\{3,4,6,10,15\},
\]
as well as the six stated primality conditions.

However, no numbers can satisfy even the displayed size, ordering, and sum conditions. Indeed, every member of \(\{3,4,6,10,15\}\) is at least \(3\), so \(x\ge 3\). Since \(x\le y\le z\), we also have
\[
y\ge x\ge 3\qquad\text{and}\qquad z\ge y\ge x\ge 3.
\]
Consequently,
\[
x+y+z\ge 3+3+3=9,
\]
contradicting the required equality \(x+y+z=7\).

Equivalently, one may spell out the finite-list alternatives. If \(x=3\), ordering forces \(y,z\ge3\), so the sum is at least \(9\). If \(x=4\), the sum is at least \(12\); if \(x=6\), at least \(18\); if \(x=10\), at least \(30\); and if \(x=15\), at least \(45\). None can equal \(7\). Thus the contradiction occurs before any primality condition needs to be considered.

Therefore the strengthened representation asserted for every integer \(n>6\) already fails at \(n=7\). Since the original conjecture universally asserts both the positivity clause and this strengthened clause, failure of the latter at a single admissible value of \(n\) disproves the entire conjecture. This conclusion does not require the positivity claim \(a(7)>0\) to fail; a universally quantified conjunction is false as soon as either conjunct fails for one value. Hence the stated conjecture is false.
